newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says car air bag cutoff ruling due soon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says car air bag cutoff ruling due soon.

text.p: U.S. car safety officials said Monday that they would decide soon on a controversial move whether to allow car owners to have air bags disconnected.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) made the disconnection proposal last year along with other steps to reduce the danger of the fast-deploying air bags, but held up a final decision because of the many public comments the proposal triggered.

NHTSA Administrator Richardo Martinez told a House of Representatives subcommittee that "We are now in the final stages of deliberations in this matter and expect to issue a final rule in the near future." But he gave no timetable.

While saving some 1,900 lives since first used, air bags are also blamed for 63 deaths. Of these, the NHTSA says, most were adults riding unbuckled or children improperly restrained. It said if not properly restrained. the fast-deploying bag -- at speeds up to 200 miles an hour -- can snap a person's neck.

Although holding up on a disconnection ruling, the NHTSA did allow car-makers to install less powerful air bags and directed them to develop a "smart" air bag that automatically shuts off when a small adult or child is in the passenger seat.
But Martinez told the House panel on telecommunications, trade and consumer protection that remedies already exist to make air bags safer, short of disconnecting them.

Remedies include enabling an adult to position his or her seat to stay at least 10-12 inches away from the airbag and to use foot pedal extenders and seat cusions if needed, and for children to always ride in the rear seat properly restrained.
With these steps, he added, deaths from high-powered air bag inflation would fall drastically. "Very few people need to avail themselves of the alternative (disconnection)," Martinez said.
The Big Three car-makers, Chrysler Corp., Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp., along with a car dealers group registered their opposition to disconnection.

Ramsay Gillman, president of the National Automobile Dealers Association, said "If NHTSA adopts a broad deactivation policy, I can guarantee you that customers will be walking into dealerships to have their air bags disconnected regardless of whether they should or not."
He backed the installation of cut-off switches for temporary deactivation when customers provide justification.
